CausalChain: Hypoxic/oxidative stress in liver -> Upregulation and m6A modification of specific lncRNAs -> Structural remodeling of lncRNAs increases their translation into micropeptides -> Micropeptides bind to HIF-1α regulatory proteins (e.g., E3 ubiquitin ligases) -> Inhibition of HIF-1α degradation -> Stabilization and activation of HIF-1α -> Enhanced angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and metastasis in HCC
Hypothesis: In HCC, hypoxia-induced m6A modifications on specific lncRNAs promote the production of micropeptides that interfere with HIF-1α degradation. This mechanism stabilizes HIF-1α and drives angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and metastasis, suggesting that targeting the m6A modification or the resultant micropeptides may offer a novel therapeutic strategy.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression has been increasingly attributed to the multifaceted roles of long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) including their interactions with proteins, RNAs, and epigenetic modifiers. Recent findings indicate that many lncRNAs are subject to dynamic N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications which alter their secondary structure and binding affinities. Additionally, a subset of lncRNAs encodes small peptides with hitherto underappreciated biological functions. In this study, we propose that under hypoxic and oxidative stress conditions characteristic of the HCC microenvironment, m6A-modified lncRNAs not only act as molecular scaffolds but also yield functional micropeptides. These peptides may directly interact with components of the HIF-1α regulatory machinery, inhibiting its degradation, thereby enhancing angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and metastasis. This hypothesis presents a novel integrative mechanism linking epitranscriptomic regulation and peptide-encoding potential of lncRNAs to the aggressive phenotypes observed in HCC.
